newsitem.title: USA: Condemned man's life in balance in California.
newsitem.headline: Condemned man's life in balance in California.

text.p: The state of California awaited word from the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday to find out if convicted killer Thomas Thompson could be executed despite a last minute reprieve from a federal appeals court.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals' decided on Sunday, less than 36 hours before the scheduled execution, to spare Thompson's life and to reverse his rape conviction. That outraged Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, who said it was the decision of a "coterie of liberal judges."

California Attorney General Dan Lungren immediately appealed to the Supreme Court to overturn the ruling and said he hoped the court would order the execution to go ahead just after midnight on Monday as previously scheduled.
State officials said they did not know when the Supreme Court would rule.
Preparations for Thompson's execution were going ahead at San Quentin State Prison in case the Supreme Court ruled in California's favour, the state Department of Corrections said.
"The preparations are moving forward as if the execution will take place," department spokeswoman Christine May said.
Reporters who had been planning to cover the execution were told to go to the prison by mid-afternoon as scheduled.

Thompson, 42, was convicted in 1983 of raping and murdering Ginger Fleischli, 20, two years earlier at his apartment in Laguna Beach in southern California, after an evening of drinking and smoking hashish. He has protested his innocence, saying he passed out after consensual sex with Fleischli.
Thompson, who faced death by lethal injection, would have been the fifth person to be executed in California since the state resumed executions in 1992.

Thompson's attorneys campaigned to spare his life, raising doubts about his rape conviction, which as a "special circumstance" in combination with murder made Thompson eligible for the death penalty under California law.
In 1995, a U.S. district judge, finding that Thompson had been inadequately represented by his attorney at his trial, threw out the rape conviction and death sentence.

But the conviction and sentence were reinstated by a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court denied Thompson's appeal, Wilson denied his clemency plea and all hope for Thompson seemed lost.
But in a surprise move, an 11-judge panel of the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals -- which has a liberal reputation -- reviewed the case again and overturned the earlier ruling.

"The consequence of our failure to act would be the execution of a person as to whom a grave question exists whether he is innocent of the death-qualifying offence, the alleged rape," the divided court said in its 7-4 ruling.

The appeals court criticised the performance of Thompson's trial attorney and said the prosecution's use of conflicting theories of the murder in the separate trials of Thompson and co-defendant David Leitch violated Thompson's right to due process.

Gregory Long, one of Thompson's attorneys, said he was very pleased with the appeals court decision. "We came perilously close to executing a man who is probably innocent of all of these crimes," he told Reuters.

The most dramatic recent legal tug-of-war over an execution in California happened in 1992 when Robert Alton Harris was strapped into the gas chamber at San Quentin only to be taken out when the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals abruptly halted the process after appeals by lawyers arguing that the gas chamber was a cruel and unusual punishment.
Harris was led back into the gas chamber and executed minutes after the Supreme Court struck down his last stay of execution.
